SubCat01_Text:
Autogenic Training is a scientifically recognized relaxation method developed in the 1920s by the Berlin psychiatrist Johannes Heinrich Schultz. It is based on self-suggestion. By repeatedly mentally reciting certain formulas, like ("My arm is very heavy" or "My breathing is calm and even"), you can put your body and mind into a state of deep relaxation.

Effects on Body and Mind
Autogenic Training can reduce stress, relieve inner tension, and enhance concentration. When practiced regularly, it supports regeneration, improves sleep, and can alleviate psychosomatic complaints. On a mental level, it helps to organize thoughts, find inner calm, and enhance well-being.

Influence on the Autonomic Nervous System
The autonomic nervous system controls vital bodily functions such as heart rate, breathing, blood pressure, and digestion – largely without our conscious intervention. Autogenic Training has a regulating effect on this system by activating the parasympathetic nervous system, which is responsible for relaxation and recovery. At the same time, the excessive activity of the sympathetic nervous system – responsible for stress reactions such as rapid heartbeat or muscle tension – is reduced.

Examples of Control through Autogenic Training
  • Cardiovascular System: By using the formula 'My heart beats calmly and regularly', pulse rate can decrease, and blood pressure and heart rate stabilize.
  • Breathing: With 'My breathing flows calmly and evenly', breathing can be deepened and slowed, promoting inner calm.
  • Muscles: 'My arms and legs are pleasantly heavy' can relieve muscle tension and induce physical relaxation.
  • Temperature Regulation: 'My right arm is very warm' influences blood circulation and can warm cold hands or feet. Through this self-regulation, Autogenic Training becomes a powerful tool to positively influence physical and mental well-being.

Anxiety-Text:
Anxiety is a natural response to stress or perceived danger, characterized by feelings of worry, nervousness, or fear. It can manifest in various forms, ranging from mild unease to severe panic attacks. While occasional anxiety is a normal part of life, chronic or excessive anxiety can interfere with daily activities and overall well-being.

Common symptoms of anxiety include:
  • Restlessness or feeling on edge
  • Rapid heartbeat
  • Excessive worrying
  • Difficulty concentrating
  • Muscle tension
  • Sleep disturbances
Anxiety disorders are the most common mental health disorders and can be triggered by a combination of genetic, environmental, and psychological factors. They often develop in response to stressful life events, trauma, or ongoing stressors.

Treatment for anxiety typically involves a combination of psychotherapy, medication, and lifestyle changes. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is particularly effective in helping individuals identify and change negative thought patterns that contribute to anxiety. Medications such as antidepressants or benzodiazepines may also be prescribed to manage symptoms. Additionally, practices like mindfulness meditation, regular exercise, and adequate sleep can help reduce anxiety levels.

GenAnxiety-Text:
Generalized Anxiety Disorder


Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a widespread mental illness characterized by persistent and excessive worries and anxieties. People with GAD often find it difficult to control their worries, which can lead to significant impairments in daily life. Typical symptoms include constant nervousness, muscle tension, sleep disturbances, and problems with concentration.

The causes of GAD are diverse and can include genetic, environmental, and psychological factors. Stressful life events, such as the loss of a loved one or professional challenges, can contribute to the development of GAD.

The treatment of Generalized Anxiety Disorder typically includes psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which aims to identify and change negative thought patterns. In some cases, medications such as antidepressants or anxiolytics may also be prescribed to alleviate the symptoms. With the right support and treatment, people with GAD can learn to manage their fears and lead a fulfilling life.

Autogenic Training can help with Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) by releasing deeply rooted physical and mental tension. The constant worry in GAD often leads to physiological symptoms like muscle tension, gastrointestinal issues, or insomnia. Through targeted autosuggestions such as “My body is completely heavy” or “My breath is calm and steady,” users learn to consciously soothe these physical reactions. This sends a relaxation signal to the nervous system and breaks the vicious cycle of anxiety and tension. On a cognitive level, autogenic training helps to stop the “thought carousel.” Users learn to shift their focus away from their worries and concentrate on the physical sensations of relaxation. This practice trains the mind to gain distance from thoughts and regain a sense of inner control. It is an active way to reduce excessive worry and sustainably improve quality of life.
Depression-Text:
Depression

Depression is a common and serious mental illness, marked by persistent sadness, loss of interest, and various emotional and physical symptoms. Everyday tasks can feel overwhelming, and many affected people struggle with feelings of hopelessness or worthlessness. Causes are diverse and may include genetic, biological, environmental, and psychological factors.

Typical symptoms of depression include:
  • Persistent sadness or emptiness
  • Loss of interest in activities once enjoyed
  • Changes in sleep or eating patterns
  • Exhaustion and lack of energy
  • Difficulty concentrating or making decisions
  • Feelings of guilt or worthlessness
  • Thoughts of death or suicide
Treatment often combines psychotherapy, medication, and self-help strategies. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) helps to identify and change negative thought patterns, while antidepressants can restore balance in the brain. With the right support, many people experience significant improvement and regain quality of life.

Common forms are the classic depressive episode, marked by low mood and lack of energy, and atypical depression, which can involve increased sleep and appetite. Autogenic Training (AT) can be supportive by bringing the body into deep relaxation. It helps calm the nervous system and regulate functions like sleep and heart rate. Through focused autosuggestions such as “My body is full of calm and strength,” negative thought patterns can be interrupted, restoring inner control and resilience. AT thus strengthens the mind-body connection and supports both mental and physical health.
